name: Lofepramine
metabolism: Lofepramine is rapidly absorbed, with peak plasma concentration reached within 1 hour and about 5 hours in the body, and like imipramine it appears to be broken down substantially on the way through the liver. Plasma protein binding is about 99%. Almost all the drug is broken down before excretion, which is mainly in the urine and in faeces. Lofepramine is broken down by N-dealkylation, hydroxylation and glucuronidation, and is extensively broken down to its principal metabolite desmethylimipramine on first pass through the liver; during chronic administration the plasma level of desmethylimipramine is typically three times greater than that of lofepramine, except in the first few hours after each dose. Desipramine, which is also an antidepressant, is converted to 2-hydroxydesipramine in the liver. Both compounds are excreted mainly in the urine as glucuronides, and also by biliary excretion in the faeces. Less than 5% is excreted unchanged in the urine over 24 hours. Elimination may be reduced and bioavailability increased in hepatic disease.
summary: Lofepramine is a tricyclic antidepressant used to treat depression. It is considered relatively safer in overdose and has milder, less frequent side effects than many other tricyclic antidepressants.
